title: Grace at meals
hookLine: bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts

lines: SO FAST IT'S ONE LONG WORD.
cards: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts." At one kitchen table, a family says it so fast it comes out as one long word, and the youngest is reaching for the potatoes before the amen.

At another, an old couple hold hands across the plates and say it slowly, the way they've said it for years. In a school cafeteria, a girl bows her head for two seconds over a tray, and nobody notices but her.
The words are short. The food is getting cold. And still, people stop, just before the first bite.

teach.h: BLESS US, O LORD, AND THESE THY GIFTS.
teach.b: The old Catholic grace goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." It doesn't call the food dinner.
It calls it gifts, named as given before anyone has tasted it. Other churches have their own graces, rhymed or spoken freely, but they tend to do the same thing. Next, Jesus at a meal.
In Mark, a hungry crowd sits on the grass with almost nothing to eat. The disciples want to send everyone away to buy food.

teach.h: HE LOOKED UP, AND BLESSED, AND BRAKE.
teach.b: Instead, Jesus takes what there is: "he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and brake the loaves." Look up, bless, break: a pause, a word of thanks, and then the food is shared. Then, an older command.

teach.h: WHEN THOU HAST EATEN AND ART FULL.
teach.b: In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee."
After the meal, when you're full, exactly when it's easiest to forget. Jewish tradition keeps a blessing after eating from this verse; Christian graces come before the meal, after it, or both.
Last, Paul to Timothy: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Grace doesn't change the food. It changes how the food is received.

how: Christians of different churches say a short grace before meals, at home or in public; Catholics often use "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts," others use their own set words or pray in their own words, and some also give thanks after eating.

o: a fast from food kept on the holy days of the year
a polite word of thanks to whoever cooked dinner
a short pause of thanks before or after eating

games.q: grace at meals — tap the pairs.
p: looked up, and blessed, and brake
when thou hast eaten and art full

s: grace before meals is only a Catholic custom
the old grace is Catholic, but other churches have graces of their own, rhymed or spoken freely.
in Mark, Jesus blesses the loaves before the crowd eats
"he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and brake the loaves."
Deuteronomy's blessing comes before the meal
it comes after: "when thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God."

games.q: you're one of the disciples. a huge crowd is hungry, and there's almost no food. what does Jesus do first?
o: send everyone away to buy their own food.
look up to heaven and bless the loaves.
start tearing the bread and handing it out.
games.why: the disciples suggested sending them away. instead, "he looked up to heaven, and blessed, and brake the loaves."

practice: Set food or a drink in front of you, or bring your next meal to mind, and trace it backward, one breath for each step: the hands that cooked it, the store, the truck, the field, the rain.
If you pray, you can say the old grace slowly, one phrase at a time; if you don't, silently name a few of the people it took to bring this food to you.

wordCard.voice: Grace at meals. A short pause of thanks before or after eating, naming the food as a gift and God as the giver.

orig.note: Greek: to bless, the verb Mark uses when Jesus blesses the loaves.

carryVoice: Your line: these thy gifts. A meal, named as given. Same time tomorrow.
